overview: Castile grew from a northern Iberian lordship into a kingdom and, after its permanent union with León in 1230, a much larger crown. Its history includes nuns with judicial authority, traveling flocks, manuscript workshops and Atlantic expansion. The atlas spellings Castilla, Castile and Castille label successive map segments, not three unrelated peoples. Their 1279, 1492 and 1530 boundaries are coverage limits.

periods.title: Before the permanent union
periods.summary: Castile and León passed through unions and divisions; they were separate monarchies again from 1157 to 1230. The early Castilla polygon is a simplified snapshot, not a complete account of territorial growth.

periods.title: The Castilian-Leonese crown
periods.summary: Ferdinand III permanently united the crowns in 1230. Expansion south brought more cities and communities under his successors.

periods.title: Dynastic union and new horizons
periods.summary: Isabella and Ferdinand linked the crowns of Castile and Aragon while their institutions remained distinct. Castile continued beyond the atlas segment.

sections.title: Books, learning and things people made

items.text: A court manuscript completed in Seville in 1283 explains chess, dice and tables. Its compiler associated chess with calculation, dice with chance, and tables with a mixture. The book drew on games transmitted through Arabic sources; Alfonso X did not invent chess.

The Book of Games survives on 97 parchment leaves with abundant paintings. A game manual could be a major artistic commission: considerably more elaborate than the instructions that disappear from a board-game box.

The Cantigas de Santa María joined poetry, music and pictures in Alfonso X’s court. The Códice Rico, c. 1280 to 1284, illustrates miracles in sequences of scenes. These are religious stories, though their artists also pictured clothing, instruments and everyday activities.

A short Galician-Portuguese sample from Cantiga 10 reads “Rosa das rosas e Fror das frores”: “Rose of roses and Flower of flowers,” praising Mary. This is a scholarly transcription of a medieval song in Latin letters, not proof that everyone spoke or read the court’s literary languages.

Salamanca’s 1254 university staffing included teachers of law, grammar, logic and medicine, as well as an apothecary and librarian. These named posts show organized advanced study, not universal schooling or evidence that medieval medical treatments worked.

Nebrija’s Castilian grammar was printed in Salamanca in 1492. One section taught the language to people with another mother tongue. Red and black ink and empty spaces for decorative initials preserve a moment when printed books still borrowed habits from manuscripts.

At Burgos, Alfonso VIII and Eleanor founded Las Huelgas in 1187 as a community of Cistercian nuns and royal burial place. Its abbess exercised unusually extensive authority, including jurisdiction over dependent properties. This was a powerful particular institution, not the position of all Castilian women.

The 1187 founding charter of Las Huelgas survives as a large parchment document with a circular royal sign and witnesses. Its Latin words “Facta carta in burgis” mean “The charter was made in Burgos.” Official writing made royal gifts and obligations durable.

Clothes from the tomb of Prince Fernando de la Cerda, who died in 1275, include a fitted laced garment, an open-sided outer garment and a fur-lined mantle. Castles and lions advertised royal identity. These costly burial clothes reveal elite fashion, not a peasant’s wardrobe.

The Mesta received royal privileges under Alfonso X in 1273. Its livestock owners and shepherds depended on grazing and passage rights. Moving animals across the landscape was skilled work with legal consequences, not simply letting sheep wander wherever they liked.

The Hospital del Rey in Burgos was founded in 1195 to assist pilgrims and sick poor people. Its later connection with Las Huelgas linked hospitality, religious endowment and care. “Hospital” could include shelter and food as well as treatment.

The 1492 expulsion decree disrupted Jewish households and communities. Archival records track the property and debts they left behind. A crown’s expansion could therefore coincide with families losing their homes; cultural exchange should not be mistaken for continuous equality or safety.

ending.text: Castile did not fall in 1492 or 1530. Dynastic union with Aragon from 1479 helped form the Spanish monarchy, while the crowns retained separate institutions. Castilian communities and institutions continued, even as conquest and religious coercion transformed many people’s lives.
